A technique is described for evaluating how exposure to different colours of light influences a person’s experience of tinnitus. The technique includes positioning a display within at least a portion of the person’s visual field, lighting that display with visible-spectrum coloured light generated by one or more adjustable light sources, changing quantifiable properties of the coloured illumination, and noting the particular measured light values at which the person reports an alteration in their tinnitus perception.

The disclosure also includes methods for identifying tristimulus light values that may reduce a person’s perception of tinnitus, methods for generating data sets containing measured values of coloured light, the use of coloured light for this purpose, articles designed to alter illumination across at least part of a person’s field of vision, a method for reducing a person’s perceived tinnitus, and the use of equipment to assess how viewing changing colours of light affects a person’s perception of tinnitus.
outputs.L3:
The method assesses how exposure to different colours of light affects a subject’s perception of tinnitus. In use, a visual display is positioned so that it occupies at least part of the subject’s field of view. The display is then illuminated, or otherwise presented, using coloured light within the visible spectrum. The colour of the light can be adjusted in a controlled manner so that the subject is exposed to a range of different visual colour conditions.

During the assessment, measurable characteristics of the coloured light are varied while the subject reports any corresponding changes in their tinnitus perception. These measurable characteristics may include colour values that define the light being viewed, such as tristimulus values or other objective colour parameters. As the subject observes each colour condition, they may indicate whether their tinnitus becomes louder, quieter, more intrusive, less intrusive, or otherwise changes in character.

The colour values associated with the subject’s reported responses are recorded. By analysing these recorded values, it is possible to identify particular tristimulus values, or ranges of values, that are associated with a reduction or alleviation of the subject’s perceived tinnitus. These values may then be used to determine visual illumination settings that are potentially beneficial for that subject.

The text also encompasses related applications and implementations. These may include uses of coloured visual illumination for assessing tinnitus, articles configured to provide such illumination, data sets containing colour values and associated tinnitus-response information, and apparatus for modifying visual illumination. Such apparatus may be used either to evaluate how different colours affect tinnitus perception or to provide selected visual illumination intended to relieve or reduce the subject’s tinnitus symptoms.
outputs.L4:
A method is provided for assessing the effect of visible light on a subject’s perception of tinnitus. The method includes presenting to the subject an illuminated display or other controllable light-emitting surface while the subject is experiencing, or is able to perceive, tinnitus. The display is operated to emit visible light having selected, measurable color characteristics. These color characteristics may be expressed, for example, as tristimulus values, chromaticity coordinates, wavelength or spectral power distribution data, hue, saturation, brightness, intensity, luminance, or other colorimetric parameters.

During the assessment, the emitted light is varied across a plurality of color conditions. The variations may be performed manually, automatically, randomly, sequentially, or according to a predetermined test protocol. For each presented color condition, the subject provides feedback indicating whether the perceived tinnitus changes. The feedback may include, without limitation, whether the tinnitus appears louder, softer, higher in pitch, lower in pitch, more intrusive, less intrusive, unchanged, masked, reduced, or otherwise altered. The subject’s response may be recorded together with the corresponding measurable color values of the displayed light.

The recorded information may then be analyzed to identify one or more color conditions associated with a perceived reduction, masking, or alleviation of tinnitus. In some implementations, the identified color conditions are represented as tristimulus values or other standardized color values so that the same or substantially similar light conditions can be reproduced later. The method may also identify color conditions that increase or otherwise adversely affect tinnitus perception, allowing such conditions to be avoided.

The collected data may be stored as an individual tinnitus-response profile for the subject. In other implementations, data from multiple subjects may be aggregated to create datasets correlating visible-light color parameters with reported tinnitus perception. Such datasets may be used to develop or configure light-emitting devices, display systems, therapeutic articles, computer-readable instructions, treatment protocols, or apparatus configured to present selected visible-light conditions to a subject.

In use, a device or apparatus may include a controllable light source, a processor, memory, and an input interface for receiving subject feedback. The processor may control the light source to present different color conditions, record the subject’s responses, determine color values associated with beneficial changes in tinnitus perception, and subsequently reproduce those color values during a light-based intervention session. The light source may be incorporated into a screen, lamp, headset, eyewear, panel, room-lighting system, wearable article, mobile device, or other illuminated article capable of producing controlled visible light.

The approach therefore enables the identification and reproduction of visible-light conditions that may reduce, mask, or otherwise alleviate a subject’s perception of tinnitus. By associating subjective tinnitus responses with objective color measurements, the method supports personalized light-based interventions as well as the creation of reproducible therapeutic settings, treatment devices, data records, and related apparatus for managing tinnitus perception.

The word **“also”** is a small but useful word in English. It is used to add information, connect ideas, and show that something is included in addition to something else. For example, if someone says, “I like reading,” they can add, “I also enjoy writing.” In this sentence, “also” helps link two related ideas smoothly.

“Also” is often used in both spoken and written English. It can make sentences sound more complete and connected. Writers use it to introduce extra details, while speakers use it to continue a thought or add another point. For instance: “The museum has beautiful paintings. It also has interesting historical exhibits.”

Although “also” is a simple word, it plays an important role in communication. It helps avoid repetition and makes ideas flow naturally. Whether in essays, conversations, emails, or stories, “also” is a helpful word for adding more information clearly and effectively.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style abstract for an invention involving testing different colors of visible light to determine their effect on a patient's tinnitus perception.
counterfactuals.output: A method and system are provided for assessing modulation of tinnitus perception using visible light stimulation. In one embodiment, a patient experiencing tinnitus is exposed to a plurality of visible light stimuli having different colors, wavelengths, intensities, durations, or temporal patterns. During or after exposure to each light stimulus, the patient provides an indication of a perceived change in tinnitus, including one or more of loudness, pitch, annoyance, laterality, masking, or suppression. The responses are recorded and correlated with the corresponding light parameters to identify one or more light conditions that alter the patient’s tinnitus perception. The identified light condition may be used to generate a patient-specific tinnitus modulation profile and, optionally, to guide subsequent therapeutic, diagnostic, or monitoring procedures. The system may include a controllable light source, a user interface for receiving patient feedback, and a processor configured to present a sequence of colored light stimuli and analyze patient responses.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a broad patent claim summary for a method and apparatus that varies tristimulus values of colored light in a subject’s visual field and records when tinnitus symptoms change.
counterfactuals.output:
A broad patent claim summary may be framed as follows:

A method and apparatus are provided for evaluating and/or modulating tinnitus by presenting controlled colored light stimuli to a subject and monitoring changes in tinnitus perception. The apparatus includes a light-generating system configured to produce light within a subject’s visual field, a controller configured to vary one or more tristimulus values of the light, and an input or recording system configured to record an indication from the subject corresponding to a perceived change in tinnitus symptoms.

In one aspect, the method includes presenting colored light to at least a portion of a subject’s visual field, varying the tristimulus values of the presented light over time, and receiving or recording data indicating when the subject perceives a change in tinnitus. The change may include an increase, decrease, masking, suppression, modulation, or other alteration in tinnitus loudness, pitch, intensity, location, annoyance, or perceptual quality.

In another aspect, the tristimulus values may correspond to color coordinates, RGB values, CIE XYZ values, chromaticity values, luminance, hue, saturation, intensity, or combinations thereof. The light may be varied continuously, stepwise, randomly, according to a predetermined sequence, or adaptively based on subject feedback.

In another aspect, the apparatus includes a visual display, light source, head-mounted display, projection system, LED array, or other optical stimulator arranged to expose the subject’s visual field to selectable colors. The controller may adjust the spectral output, intensity, duration, spatial pattern, temporal modulation, or field position of the colored light. A user interface, sensor, button, touchscreen, voice input, physiological sensor, or other data capture device may be used to record the time or condition at which tinnitus symptoms change.

In another aspect, the recorded data may be associated with the tristimulus values present at or near the time of the reported tinnitus change, thereby identifying one or more color conditions correlated with tinnitus modulation for the subject. The system may store, analyze, rank, or reproduce such color conditions for diagnostic, therapeutic, calibration, research, or personalization purposes.

In another aspect, the apparatus may further include memory and processing circuitry configured to generate a tinnitus-response profile for the subject based on the recorded changes and corresponding light parameters. The profile may be used to select subsequent colored-light stimuli, refine a stimulation protocol, or provide repeated exposure to one or more color settings associated with beneficial tinnitus change.

An exemplary broad independent method claim could be summarized as:

A method comprising: presenting colored light within a visual field of a subject; varying tristimulus values of the colored light; receiving an indication that a tinnitus symptom perceived by the subject has changed; and recording data associating the indication with the tristimulus values of the colored light.

An exemplary broad independent apparatus claim could be summarized as:

An apparatus comprising: a light output device configured to present colored light within a visual field of a subject; a controller configured to vary tristimulus values of the colored light; and a recording interface configured to record an indication of a change in a tinnitus symptom of the subject in association with the tristimulus values.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an intellectual property abstract describing the use of variable colored illumination, displays, and data sets to assess and alleviate tinnitus.
counterfactuals.output:
An apparatus and method are provided for assessing and alleviating tinnitus through controlled presentation of variable colored illumination and/or visual display content. In one embodiment, a user interface presents selectable or automatically varied colors, luminance levels, saturation levels, temporal modulation patterns, spatial patterns, images, or video sequences to a subject experiencing tinnitus. The subject’s perceived tinnitus intensity, pitch, annoyance, masking response, relaxation response, or other subjective or physiological response is recorded and associated with corresponding visual stimulus parameters in a data set. The data set may be analyzed to identify visual characteristics that correlate with reduction, masking, habituation, distraction, relaxation, or aggravation of tinnitus symptoms.

The system may include one or more light sources, display screens, wearable displays, room illumination devices, mobile computing devices, sensors, processors, memory, and software configured to generate test sequences and therapeutic sessions. Stimulus parameters may be adjusted manually by the subject, prescribed by a clinician, or automatically optimized using stored response data, machine learning, adaptive algorithms, or population-based data sets. In some embodiments, auditory stimuli, biofeedback, questionnaires, sleep data, stress indicators, heart rate variability, electroencephalographic data, or environmental information are combined with visual-response data to refine assessment and therapy.

The identified colors, brightness ranges, display patterns, or illumination sequences may be used in personalized treatment protocols intended to reduce perceived tinnitus severity, improve attention, promote relaxation, facilitate sleep, or support habituation therapy. Aggregated data sets may further be used to classify tinnitus profiles, predict effective visual stimulus parameters, monitor symptom changes over time, and generate recommendations for individualized illumination or display-based interventions.

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal patent language, describe a method of assessing whether viewing different colours of light can reduce or alter a subject’s perception of tinnitus.
counterfactuals.output:
A method of assessing an effect of chromatic visual stimulation on tinnitus perception in a subject, the method comprising:

1. obtaining, from the subject, a baseline tinnitus-perception indication representative of at least one perceived characteristic of tinnitus, the at least one perceived characteristic comprising one or more of perceived loudness, pitch, intrusiveness, annoyance, discomfort, masking, laterality, or awareness;

2. presenting to the subject, by a light-output device, a plurality of visual stimuli having respectively different colour characteristics, wherein each visual stimulus comprises light having at least one predetermined spectral property selected from wavelength, dominant wavelength, correlated colour temperature, hue, saturation, luminance, intensity, bandwidth, or chromaticity coordinates;

3. during or after presentation of each of the plurality of visual stimuli, receiving from the subject a tinnitus-response indication corresponding to the subject’s perceived tinnitus while viewing or having viewed the respective visual stimulus;

4. comparing the tinnitus-response indication for each respective visual stimulus with the baseline tinnitus-perception indication and/or with tinnitus-response indications associated with other visual stimuli; and

5. determining, based on the comparison, whether at least one colour characteristic of light produces a reduction, increase, modulation, or other alteration in the subject’s perception of tinnitus.

In certain embodiments, the method further comprises presenting the plurality of visual stimuli in a randomized, pseudo-randomized, or predetermined sequence. Each visual stimulus may be presented for a predetermined exposure interval, optionally separated by a rest interval or a neutral-light interval. The light-output device may comprise a display screen, light-emitting diode array, head-mounted display, lamp, projector, or other controllable illumination source.

In further embodiments, the baseline tinnitus-perception indication and the tinnitus-response indication are obtained by one or more user inputs, including a numerical rating, visual analogue scale, categorical selection, questionnaire response, verbal response, touchscreen input, button input, slider input, or physiological or behavioural measurement correlated with tinnitus perception.

In some embodiments, the method comprises controlling one or more non-colour parameters of the visual stimuli, including brightness, luminance, duration, viewing distance, ambient illumination, flicker, spatial pattern, or field size, such that differences in tinnitus-response indications are attributable at least in part to differences in colour characteristic.

In further embodiments, the method comprises identifying a subject-specific colour or range of colours associated with a decreased tinnitus-perception indication relative to the baseline indication. The method may further comprise storing the identified colour characteristic in a memory, generating a subject-specific tinnitus-modulation profile, and outputting a recommendation or control signal for subsequent presentation of light having the identified colour characteristic.

In one embodiment, the comparing step comprises determining a tinnitus modulation value for each visual stimulus, the tinnitus modulation value being based on a difference between the baseline tinnitus-perception indication and the tinnitus-response indication. A visual stimulus may be classified as tinnitus-reducing when the tinnitus modulation value satisfies a predetermined criterion, such as a reduction exceeding a threshold percentage, score, or statistically significant difference.

In another embodiment, the method further comprises repeating presentation of at least one visual stimulus on multiple occasions and determining whether the alteration in tinnitus perception is reproducible across repeated presentations. The method may additionally comprise excluding or flagging responses affected by fatigue, adaptation, ambient noise, visual discomfort, migraine symptoms, photophobia, or inconsistent subject reporting.

Thus, the method provides a structured assessment of whether viewing different colours of light reduces, increases, or otherwise alters a subject’s subjective perception of tinnitus, and may identify one or more colour parameters associated with tinnitus modulation for that subject.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a patent application abstract for an apparatus and method using coloured light sources to identify light values that may alleviate tinnitus in human subjects.
counterfactuals.output: An apparatus and method are provided for identifying one or more light values associated with alleviation of tinnitus in a human subject. The apparatus includes a plurality of controllable colored light sources, a controller configured to vary one or more light parameters including wavelength, color, intensity, saturation, brightness, pulse frequency, duty cycle, and exposure duration, and a user interface configured to receive subject feedback relating to perceived tinnitus severity during or after exposure to selected light values. In use, the subject is exposed to a sequence of colored-light stimuli while tinnitus-related responses are recorded. The controller correlates the selected light values with the subject feedback to identify at least one candidate light value or light-value range that produces a reduction in perceived tinnitus loudness, annoyance, or discomfort. The identified light value may be stored as a subject-specific therapeutic profile and subsequently reproduced by the apparatus for further testing or treatment sessions. The method may include adaptive adjustment of the light stimuli based on real-time subject feedback to refine the therapeutic profile.
